description.sr_latin: Kako da kažeš šta misliš i kako se osećaš — bez filtera.
description.en: How to say what you think and how you feel — unfiltered.

phrases.context: Your friend lays out a plan and you're fully on board — give the plain, standard yes.
phrases.notes: 'Slagati se' is reflexive — the 'se' is mandatory and can never be dropped.

phrases.context: Your friend sums up the situation perfectly and you want to confirm it in one quick word.
phrases.notes: 'Tačno' = exact/correct (neuter adverb here). Same root as 'tačka' = dot/point.

phrases.context: Your friend phrases your own point even sharper than you did — back them up emphatically.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' = exactly/really, an intensifier you'll hear constantly; 'tako' = like that.

phrases.context: Your friend makes a fair point in a disagreement and you want to concede that they've got it.
phrases.notes: Fixed phrase 'biti u pravu' = to be right, with 'pravo' in the locative. Word order: clitic 'si' sits second.

phrases.context: Your friend floats an idea you find totally absurd and you want to wave it off on the spot.
phrases.notes: 'Ma' is a dismissive particle; 'kakvi' is literally 'what kind' turned into a flat rejection. Tone can be playful or firm.

phrases.context: Your friend describes how something went, but they've got a detail off and you gently correct them.
phrases.notes: 'Nije' is the negative of 'je' (a separate word, not 'ne' + 'je'). Soft, non-confrontational correction.

phrases.context: Your friend states an opinion you see completely differently — say so directly but stay calm.
phrases.notes: Negation by 'ne' before the verb; the reflexive 'se' stays attached. The direct opposite of 'slažem se'.

phrases.context: Your friend says something you think is total nonsense — push back with full eye-roll energy.
phrases.notes: 'Ma daj' alone is already a classic dismissal; 'molim te' (lit. 'I beg you') adds exasperation, not politeness here.

phrases.context: Your friend drops some surprising news on you and you want to check they're actually for real.
phrases.notes: 'Stvarno' = really/truly. Said flat as a statement, 'Stvarno.', it means 'for real'.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you something so shocking that it knocks the wind out of you for a second.
phrases.notes: 'Mogu da + present' renders English 'can + infinitive'; Serbian avoids the bare infinitive here. Also lands sarcastically.

phrases.context: Your friend says something you half-suspect is a joke and you want to make sure they mean it.
phrases.notes: 'Ozbiljno' = seriously (neuter adverb of 'ozbiljan'). A touch more pointed than 'stvarno'.

phrases.context: A plan changes in a way you don't love, but you give in and signal you'll go along with it.
phrases.notes: 'Pa' is a filler 'well'; 'dobro' = fine/good (neuter). Tone carries it, from mild resignation to barely held-in anger.

phrases.en: It's annoying me. / It's boring me.
phrases.context: Some task or person keeps grinding at your patience and you want to grumble about it.
phrases.notes: 'Me' is the accusative clitic — the thing is the subject, you're the object. Noun 'smaranje' = the annoyance itself. Very casual.

phrases.en: I can't anymore. / I've had enough.
phrases.context: A long, draining day or task has worn you all the way down and you want to say you're done.
phrases.notes: 'Više' = more/anymore; with negation it means 'no longer'. Works for anything you're fed up with.

phrases.context: One specific thing keeps getting under your skin and you want to name it plainly.
phrases.notes: 'To' (that) is the subject, 'me' the accusative object — lit. 'that irritates me'. From the same root as 'nervi' = nerves.

phrases.context: Your friend shares news that genuinely thrills you and you react with full enthusiasm.
phrases.notes: 'Odlično' = excellent (neuter adverb). Also the top school grade (a 5), so it carries real 'top marks' weight.

phrases.context: You hear good news about someone you care about and you want to show real warmth.
phrases.notes: Dative-experiencer: lit. 'it is dear to me', with 'mi' (to me) as the clitic experiencer. 'Drago mi je' is also 'nice to meet you'.

phrases.context: A trip, an event, or seeing someone is coming up and you're buzzing with anticipation.
phrases.notes: Literally 'I barely wait' — 'jedva' = barely/hardly. The everyday way to say you can't wait.

phrases.context: Your friend announces something painfully obvious and you want to mock it with fake amazement.
phrases.notes: 'Nemoj' is literally the prohibitive 'don't', but paired with 'ma' it flips fully sarcastic.

phrases.context: Someone pulls off something impressive — or botches it badly — and you respond with this, tone deciding which.
phrases.notes: Literally 'every honor'; 'čast' = honor. One of the most versatile phrases — pure praise or pure sarcasm by tone alone.

phrases.context: Your friend does or says something genuinely dumb and you needle them about how clever they are.
phrases.notes: 'Pametan' = smart (masculine); for a woman it's 'pametna'. Nearly always sarcastic in this frame.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you their weekend plan and you give it a relaxed nod of approval.
phrases.notes: 'Kul' is English 'cool' spelled phonetically. You'll also hear 'ekstra' for the same casual approval.

phrases.context: Your friend describes an outing that sounds deadly dull and you want to call it a snooze.
phrases.notes: 'Smor' = a bore/drag, from 'smoriti se' (to get bored). Slangy and very common among younger speakers.

phrases.context: You just sat through an endless, soul-draining meeting and you want to vent how dead it left you.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it kills me into concept' — 'pojam' = concept. An expressive, very Serbian way to say something is brutally tedious.

phrases.context: Your friend shows you something seriously cool and you want to react like it's seriously cool.
phrases.notes: 'Strava' literally means horror/dread, but it's flipped positive in slang — like English 'sick' or 'wicked'.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you their whole weekend fell apart and you react with dramatic sympathy.
phrases.notes: 'Užas' = horror/terror, but tossed out freely for everyday disasters, big or small.

phrases.context: You spot something unbearably adorable — a puppy, a baby, your girlfriend doing something cute.
phrases.notes: Dative 'mi' marks whose heart: lit. 'the heart melts to me'. 'Topiti se' = to melt (reflexive).

phrases.context: Something wonderful just happened — an engagement, a promotion — and you're bursting with it.
phrases.notes: 'Presrećan' = overjoyed (masculine); a woman says 'presrećna'. The prefix 'pre-' means 'overly', intensifying 'srećan' = happy.

phrases.context: You're venting to a friend about a guy who got right under your skin earlier today.
phrases.notes: Past tense agrees with the subject's gender: 'iznervirao' (he), 'iznervirala' (she), 'iznerviralo' (it).

phrases.context: Your partner asks what you thought of the movie you just watched and you tell them you're into it.
phrases.notes: Dative-experiencer: the thing 'sviđa se' (pleases) and you're the dative 'meni' (to me). Fronting 'meni' adds emphasis but is optional.

phrases.context: A friend asks how the restaurant was and you want to say you weren't impressed without trashing it.
phrases.notes: Dative 'mi' again: lit. 'it's not something to me'. A perfectly diplomatic, very common way to underwhelm.

phrases.en: In my opinion, that makes no sense.
phrases.context: You want to flag a take as your own before saying something just doesn't add up to you.
phrases.notes: 'Po meni' = in my view, with 'po' + dative. 'Nema' forces the genitive 'smisla' — negated 'imati' always takes the genitive.

phrases.context: Someone keeps pushing their opinion on you and you want to tell them bluntly you couldn't care less.
phrases.notes: Literally 'my ear hurts' — 'uvo' = ear. There's a cruder body-part version that's even more common.

phrases.en: I'm not so sure about that.
phrases.context: You have real doubts about what your friend just claimed but you'd rather not pick a fight.
phrases.notes: Lit. 'I don't really know'; 'baš' here softens it into polite skepticism rather than a flat 'no'.

phrases.context: You're half-persuaded by your friend's argument and willing to give a little ground without fully folding.
phrases.notes: 'Možda' = maybe softens the concession; 'u pravu' keeps 'pravo' in the locative as in 'u pravu si'.

phrases.context: You're stalling for a beat before delivering an opinion you know your friend won't want to hear.
phrases.notes: Dative 'ti' = to you. Lit. 'how should I tell you'; a classic hedge that signals something awkward is coming.
